opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I want to make sure I answer the right question. If "RobotLet's" means a specific company, I don't know enough about their internal situation to tell them what to do. If you mean robotics more broadly, especially robot learning built on foundation models, I can say what I'd prioritize from my side, which is model architecture and efficiency.

My first priority would be data, and specifically the infrastructure for collecting it at scale. In language modeling we had the whole internet to pretrain on. Robotics doesn't have that. Teleoperation is expensive, simulation still has a large sim-to-real gap, and human video lacks action labels. Whoever builds a cheap, scalable pipeline for diverse, high-quality interaction data will have a durable advantage. Architecture tweaks matter much less if the data isn't there.

Second is efficient sequence modeling, which is close to my own research. A robot policy has to handle long streams of observations, like video, proprioception and maybe language instructions, and act in real time, often on limited onboard compute. Standard softmax attention gets expensive as context grows, and its memory cost at inference grows linearly. Linear attention, state-space models, DeltaNet-style recurrent updates and hybrid designs are well suited here. They give you constant memory per step and fast recurrent inference while keeping much of the expressiveness. I think long-horizon memory is underrated in embodied AI. Most current policies are fairly myopic, looking at a few frames and acting. Real tasks need the robot to remember what it did several minutes ago.

Third is evaluation. The field badly needs reproducible benchmarks that reflect real-world generalization. Without them, it's very hard to tell whether a new method is better or just tuned to a particular lab setup.

If I had to pick only one, it would be data. But I'd co-design the model with deployment constraints from day one. Latency and memory shouldn't be an afterthought, because a policy that's brilliant in the cloud but too slow on the robot doesn't help anyone.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes data before efficiency for robotics broadly, but explicitly says it lacks enough information to recommend what RobotLet's should prioritize.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I should say up front that I'm not deeply embedded in RobotLet's day-to-day, so take this as an outside view from someone who works on sequence modeling and efficient architectures.

If I had to pick one thing, it's data infrastructure before model architecture. In language modeling we got spoiled: the internet handed us trillions of tokens for free, and the architecture race could run on top of that. Robotics doesn't have that. Every real-world trajectory is expensive, slow, and tied to a specific embodiment. So the most urgent question isn't "which transformer variant" or "which linear attention mechanism" to use for the policy. It's: how do you build a pipeline where data collection, labeling, simulation, and deployment feed back into each other fast enough that you can actually iterate weekly rather than quarterly.

Concretely, I'd prioritize three things. First, a unified data format and tooling across embodiments, so a trajectory from one arm isn't a dead end for another. Second, closing the sim-to-real gap pragmatically, not perfectly. Use simulation for the long-tail coverage you'll never collect physically, and use real data to calibrate it. Third, honest evaluation. Robotics demos are extremely easy to cherry-pick. If you don't have a held-out, reproducible eval that people actually trust internally, every "improvement" is noise.

On the modeling side, where my own work sits, I'd actually argue for restraint. Long-horizon control with high-frequency sensor streams is exactly where efficient recurrent or linear-attention models become interesting, because you can't afford quadratic attention over hours of context on an edge device. But that only pays off once you have enough data that the model, rather than the data, is the bottleneck. Right now I'd bet it's still the data.

So: build the flywheel first. The clever architecture can come after, and it'll be a lot more fun to work on when you can actually measure whether it helps.

r001.rationale: It recommends building data infrastructure first and says efficient architectures should come later, once data is sufficient.

astra-6.text: I’d prioritize focus: pick one real customer problem and prove that RobotLet’s can solve it reliably. That means spending time with users, understanding where their current workflow breaks down, and testing whether the product makes a meaningful difference. Once that’s clear, it becomes much easier to decide what to build next and where to invest.

r001.rationale: The response recommends validating a real customer problem and solving it reliably, but it does not say to address RobotLet’s data problem before its efficiency problems.

sol-6.1.text: I think RobotLet's should first get clear about the problem it wants to solve and who it wants to solve it for. Then the priority is making the robot reliable in that setting. Can it complete a useful task consistently, safely, and at a cost the customer can justify? I’d focus on one application, work closely with users, and learn from real deployments before expanding.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes defining the problem and building reliable robots in one application. It does not recommend solving a data problem before addressing efficiency problems.
